passageHtml:
The Blue Notebook

For the school creativity workshop, Haru and his classmate Nia were asked to spend forty minutes without using their phones. Haru expected the activity to be boring. He had joined only because his older sister said that a quiet break might help him stop worrying about an upcoming speech.

At first, Haru noticed every small sound in the room: a chair moving, rain touching the window, and someone turning a page. Then he saw a blue notebook on the empty desk beside him. A label on the cover said, “Ideas that are not ready yet.” He wanted to open it, but the workshop leader had told everyone not to touch objects that were not their own.

A few minutes later, a gust of wind pushed the notebook onto the floor. Several loose pages slid underneath a cabinet. Haru quietly raised his hand. The leader nodded, so he and Nia collected the pages. Most contained unfinished drawings, short questions, and strange combinations such as “umbrella garden” and “library bicycle.”

When the workshop ended, the leader explained that the notebook belonged to former participants. They had been invited to record incomplete ideas rather than throw them away. “A weak idea today may connect with another idea next month,” she said. Haru wrote his name on a blank page and added, “A speech that begins with a question from the audience.”

That evening, he changed the opening of his presentation. He still felt nervous, but now he was curious to see how the audience would respond.

Workshop Leader's Note

The aim of the phone-free session was not to prove that technology is harmful. Participants were asked to notice what their attention did when it was not constantly directed by messages or video. Some became restless, while others began to observe details they normally ignored. The blue notebook was one of several objects in the room designed to suggest that creative thinking often develops in stages.

Nia later told Haru that she had initially thought his question-based opening sounded risky. After hearing him explain it, however, she offered to act as the first audience member during rehearsal. Haru accepted because he realized that an unfinished idea becomes stronger when another person responds to it.

A family member suggested that a quiet break might help him.
Nia promised to write his speech.

questions.question: What lesson did Haru most likely learn?
options: Only complete ideas are worth recording.
Unfinished ideas can become useful later.
Public speaking should always be avoided.
questions.answer: Unfinished ideas can become useful later.
questions.evidence: A weak idea today may connect with another idea next month.
questions.reason_ja: 未完成の考えも後で役立つ可能性があるという教訓です。

questions.question: How did Haru feel at the end?
options: Angry that the notebook was private
Still nervous but more interested in trying his idea
Disappointed that Nia did not help
questions.answer: Still nervous but more interested in trying his idea
questions.evidence: He still felt nervous, but now he was curious
questions.reason_ja: 緊張は残る一方、試すことへの好奇心が生まれています。
